title: This portfolio
deck: From a NestJS API with template data to a static site fed by GitHub: mobile Lighthouse performance from 71 to 98, 86% less weight and automatic checks on every deploy.

blocks.text: The portfolio started as a template: an Astro site querying a NestJS API whose data was hand-written in TypeScript. Running a server just to serve static content added nothing, and every text change required a backend deploy.

It was also slow on mobile: the original photo weighed 1.1 MB, a fake 0–100% counter covered the hero, and an animated mascot kept the main thread busy from the first frame. Lighthouse scored it 71 for performance.

Three repositories, one responsibility each. Content lives as per-language JSON in `portafolio-api`; the brand in `me`; the site in `portafolio-web`. The root repo ties them together as git submodules.

blocks.text: **1. Reuse the existing port instead of rewriting.** The site already depended on a `PortfolioSource` interface with a mock implementation that filtered in memory. The GitHub source reuses those same filters: only where the data comes from changes.

blocks.caption: The NestJS API was replaced by ~90 lines that read JSON from GitHub.

blocks.text: **2. Render at build, revalidate on the client.** The HTML is generated with the real data (search engines and readers without JavaScript see everything). In the browser the home fetches the JSON again when idle and repaints only if something changed since the deploy.

**3. A facade for the mascot.** Its 3D animation cost 3.2 s of CPU during load. Now a static frame is drawn with the same library and the real animation starts on the first interaction: it looks identical and the load stays free.

blocks.caption: Facade pattern: same look, zero animation until someone interacts.

blocks.text: **4. No layout reads on every scroll.** The scrollspy and reveal animations read `getBoundingClientRect` on every event (667 ms of CPU during load). They now use `IntersectionObserver`; the scrollspy watches a 1 px band under the header.

blocks.text: **5. What I measured and dropped.** Preloading the headline font looked like an obvious win. An A/B test (5 runs per variant) showed the opposite: on a slow network it competed with the CSS and pushed the case LCP from 988 ms to 2,424 ms. It was removed.

blocks.text: Home FCP rises from 1.36 s to 1.74 s, and it is fair to say why: before, the first thing painted was the fake counter, not content. Today the first paint is already the full hero, and LCP —when the main content is visible— drops from 5.6 s to 2.0 s.

On mobile the hero fills exactly one screen. Content sits at the top and the leftover space holds the mascot stage, which adapts to the available height through a *container query*; on short phones it hides and the mascot appears in the corner after the hero, without covering the buttons.

blocks.text: Every push to `main` builds the site, publishes it to GitHub Pages and then runs **Lighthouse CI** against the deployed pages (3 runs per page). The workflow fails if performance drops below 90, if accessibility, best practices or SEO drop below 95, or if LCP exceeds 2.5 s.

blocks.caption: lighthouserc.json: the thresholds that guard performance.

blocks.text: **The CI has already earned its place.** It failed on its first run: the certifications page, which I had not measured, scored 75 for performance with a CLS of 0.70. It arrived empty and filled on the client, and the font swap then shifted the whole list. I built it at build time with the same renderer the client uses and added a fallback font with Sora's metrics (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, computed with fontTools).

blocks.caption: Fig. 5 — /certificaciones before (Lighthouse CI in production) and after (local Lighthouse).

blocks.text: The data repo has its own CI: a dependency-free script checks that every JSON parses, that Spanish and English have the same files and that links between cases exist.

items: **Tool:** Lighthouse 12.8.2 (CLI), default mobile profile: Moto G Power, simulated Slow 4G and 4× slower CPU.
**Fair comparison:** the previous version (commit `f15df52`) and the current one were built with the same data and served by the same gzip server, like GitHub Pages.
**Median of 3 runs** per page and version; the font test used 5 runs per variant.
**Diagnosis:** CPU profiles via the DevTools protocol on an unminified build to locate every costly function.

quote: Measure first, then change; and whatever doesn't move the number gets removed.
